Call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, severe chest pain, collapse, a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow your oncology unit’s written urgent-contact plan for other new or worsening symptoms; do not wait for the next appointment.

agents.name: Vismodegib
agents.explanation: Vismodegib blocks Smoothened, a protein in the Hedgehog signalling pathway. Abnormal activity in this pathway can drive basal cell cancer. Blocking it can slow tumour growth, while effects on normal tissues help explain cramps, taste changes and hair loss.
agents.watch: Keep four-week blood tests and the pregnancy-prevention programme. Report cramps, loss of strength, reduced intake, weight loss and severe skin symptoms.
risks: Altered or lost taste and poor appetite
Severe harm to pregnancy; prolonged prevention requirements

anatomy_note: The established anatomical illustration links body areas to the full regimen-specific descriptions. A body location helps explain possible effects; it does not diagnose the cause of a symptom or indicate its frequency.
anatomy: Tiredness can affect daily tasks. Tell the team if it worsens or comes with dizziness, reduced eating or other new symptoms.
Hair may thin or fall out. Ask about scalp care, sun protection and practical support; the timing of recovery varies.
Taste may change or disappear, making food less appealing. Report reduced intake early and ask for dietitian help.
A rash with blistering, peeling, mouth sores or fever needs urgent assessment. Keep scheduled skin reviews and report new lesions.
Cramps and muscle pain are common concerns. Severe pain, weakness or dark urine needs urgent advice; do not add supplements or medicines yourself.
Nausea, diarrhoea or constipation may occur. Call if symptoms persist, you cannot drink or urine becomes reduced.
Taste changes and poor appetite can cause weight loss. Keep a practical eating plan and tell the team about loose clothes or falling weight.
A strict pregnancy-prevention programme applies to women and men, with restrictions continuing after treatment. Report possible exposure immediately.
Report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, unusual itching or upper-abdominal pain. Keep the planned liver blood tests; a symptom needs assessment rather than self-diagnosis.

support.title: Formal pregnancy-prevention programme
support.text: The programme materials, supervised tests, contraceptive methods and after-treatment restrictions must be agreed and documented before the first dose; they apply even during a treatment pause.

support.title: An individual symptom plan
support.text: Ask which anti-sickness or other symptom medicines are prescribed, when to take them and when to call if they do not help. Do not start a borrowed medicine or alter treatment to manage a side effect yourself.

support.title: Your urgent contacts
support.text: Keep your actual oncology, out-of-hours and pharmacy contacts on the wallet card. Example numbers on a template must be replaced before you use it.

support.title: Pregnancy and fertility precautions
support.text: Vismodegib can cause severe harm to an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant need the formal pregnancy-prevention programme, including two recommended contraceptive methods (one highly effective method plus a barrier method), unless the agreed alternative is continuous abstinence, during treatment and for 24 months after stopping. Pregnancy tests are supervised before treatment and monthly, even with absent periods. Men must use a condom, with spermicide if available, during sex with a female partner during treatment and for two months afterwards, including after a vasectomy. Report a suspected patient or partner pregnancy immediately. Do not breastfeed or donate blood during treatment or for 24 months afterwards; do not donate semen during treatment or for two months afterwards. Ask the team to explain and document the full programme; this summary does not replace its materials.

support.title: Eating, activity and practical help
support.text: Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.

evidence.title: Evidence in advanced basal cell carcinoma
evidence.intro: ERIVANCE studied vismodegib without a comparison treatment. At an analysis 21 months after the last person joined the study, independent reviewers found a confirmed response in 11 of 33 people with metastatic BCC (33.3%; 95% CI 19.2-51.8%) and 30 of 63 with locally advanced BCC (47.6%; 95% CI 35.5-60.6%). The analysis date does not mean everyone took treatment for 21 months.
evidence.population: These are separate groups with advanced BCC. The response analysis included 96 people; 104 received treatment overall.
evidence.interpretation: A response means that the study's cancer-response criteria were met. The assessment combined scans for metastatic disease and lesion measurements, ulcer healing and biopsy information for locally advanced disease. Response is not the same as cure and does not prove longer survival compared with another treatment.
limitations: This study had no comparison-treatment group.
The two cancer groups and their response definitions differ.
These results used independent review at a specific analysis; later figures assessed by treating investigators must not be mixed with them.
A study result cannot predict your own benefit.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment goal
chapters.intro: Use these questions with your own pathology report and agreed treatment plan.

items.title: Confirm the diagnosis and extent
items.text: Basal cell carcinoma starts in the skin. It usually grows locally; spread to distant organs is uncommon. Your team assesses the affected area and whether surgery or radiotherapy can treat it.

items.title: Why tablets are being considered
items.text: Vismodegib is used in the advanced basal cell carcinoma settings specified in your treatment protocol. Ask the team to explain why this medicine is suitable and why an operation or radiotherapy alone is not the agreed option.

items.title: Record earlier local treatment
items.text: Record previous operations, radiotherapy and other treatment to the same area. These details help the team plan further treatment and interpret changes in the skin.

items.title: Inherited conditions and multiple cancers
items.text: Several basal cell cancers at a young age or a suggestive family history may warrant a genetics assessment. Gorlin syndrome is one possible inherited cause. Testing is selected for the person; it is not required for every skin cancer.

items.title: A visible lesion is only one part of assessment
items.text: The team may measure or photograph a visible lesion and examine deeper tissue or lymph nodes. Scans are used when they answer a specific question. A photograph alone cannot show the full extent of disease.

chapters.title: Your medicines and the overall plan
chapters.intro: Vismodegib is used to help control advanced basal cell skin cancer when the source-specific criteria are met. Discuss whether the aim is shrinkage, symptom relief, longer disease control or another agreed goal, and how surgery or radiotherapy has been considered.

items.title: The schedule in this setting
items.text: Take vismodegib once every day at the same time, continuously while the team considers it beneficial and tolerable. A 28-day calendar organises the four-week review; it is not a planned seven-day break or a fixed number of courses.

items.title: How the treatment works
items.text: Vismodegib blocks Smoothened, a protein in the Hedgehog signalling pathway. Abnormal activity in this pathway can drive basal cell cancer. Blocking it can slow tumour growth, while effects on normal tissues help explain cramps, taste changes and hair loss.

items.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
items.text: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

items.title: Pauses and stopping
items.text: A safety pause is an active treatment decision. Record which medicine is paused, the reason, the tests or recovery needed and who may authorise restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription or reset the history when a new phase begins.

chapters.title: Taking treatment and preparing for visits
chapters.intro: Keep the written medicine plan beside this guide; it records your own dose and dates.

items.title: Taking or receiving the medicine
items.text: Swallow the prescribed capsule whole with about 200 mL of water, with or without food, at the same time each day. Do not open, crush or chew it. Keep it in its labelled pack, away from children, and return unused capsules to the pharmacy.

items.title: Missed, vomited or held treatment
items.text: If a dose is missed, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not double up. If you vomit after taking it, ask the oncology team or pharmacist before taking more; do not assume that the dose needs replacing.

items.title: Other medicines and supplements
items.text: Show the pharmacist a current list of prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, herbal products and supplements. Include anticoagulants, heart medicines, steroids and recent antibiotics. Check before adding, stopping or changing anything; an apparently harmless product can alter treatment or confuse a symptom assessment.

items.title: Practical preparation
items.text: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

chapters.title: Tests: what is required and what each result means
chapters.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and response scans answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests; medicine review and pregnancy-prevention programme assessment for women and men. If pregnancy is possible, a supervised pregnancy test is needed within seven days before starting.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests every four weeks. Review cramps, strength, taste, eating, weight, hair/skin changes and treatment tolerance. Pregnancy testing is monthly when applicable, even if periods stop.

items.title: Scans and tumour markers
items.text: Ask the team to write the next assessment and who will arrange it. Bloods used to monitor kidneys, liver, hormones or muscle are not automatically measures of cancer response. There is no universal tumour-marker blood schedule for these skin-cancer regimens; a scan or extra blood test is requested for a specific clinical reason.

items.title: After a pause or finish
items.text: Agree continuing clinical/skin review, any response imaging and support for ongoing effects. The pregnancy-prevention, donation and breastfeeding restrictions continue after the last dose for their specified periods.

items.title: Getting the result
items.text: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

chapters.title: What to expect between visits
chapters.intro: You can feel well and still need the planned checks. New symptoms deserve attention even on a day without an appointment.

items.title: Your usual pattern
items.text: Record the start and change in symptoms, temperature if advised, bowel pattern, drinking, urine and the effect on normal tasks. A simple few-line record is enough. Use it to describe a change rather than trying to grade or diagnose a toxicity yourself.

items.title: When to call
items.text: Call urgently for blistering or peeling skin, mouth sores with rash or fever, severe muscle pain or weakness, or dark urine. Seek immediate advice about suspected pregnancy or exposure. Report taste change, reduced eating and weight loss early so support can start.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

items.title: A held dose and a new phase
items.text: If a dose is missed, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not double up. If you vomit after taking it, ask the oncology team or pharmacist before taking more; do not assume that the dose needs replacing.

chapters.title: Skin checks, sun protection and optional photographs
chapters.intro: This complements clinical assessment and does not replace it.

items.title: Protect your skin
items.text: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.

items.title: Know the pattern of your skin
items.text: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

items.title: Photographs are optional
items.text: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

items.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
items.text: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

chapters.title: Pregnancy, fertility and protecting others
chapters.intro: Discuss these precautions before treatment even if pregnancy is not currently planned.

items.title: Medicine-specific precautions
items.text: Vismodegib can cause severe harm to an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant need the formal pregnancy-prevention programme, including two recommended contraceptive methods (one highly effective method plus a barrier method), unless the agreed alternative is continuous abstinence, during treatment and for 24 months after stopping. Pregnancy tests are supervised before treatment and monthly, even with absent periods. Men must use a condom, with spermicide if available, during sex with a female partner during treatment and for two months afterwards, including after a vasectomy. Report a suspected patient or partner pregnancy immediately. Do not breastfeed or donate blood during treatment or for 24 months afterwards; do not donate semen during treatment or for two months afterwards. Ask the team to explain and document the full programme; this summary does not replace its materials.

items.title: Planning ahead
items.text: Ask early about fertility preservation, sexual health and symptoms affecting intimacy. Tell the team about any chance of pregnancy, breastfeeding or a partner’s pregnancy so that the correct medicine-specific advice can be given. Keep the precautions and their end dates in the written plan.

items.title: Safe handling and supply
items.text: Do not share anticancer medicines. Keep oral medicines in their original labelled packaging, away from children and anyone who could take them accidentally. Return unused medicines to the supplying pharmacy and follow its handling advice. A treatment hold does not remove pregnancy precautions.

items.title: Testing and medicine supply
items.text: When pregnancy is possible, the initial prescription and dispensing must occur by day seven, counting the pregnancy-test date as day one. Supplies are limited to 28 days and need a renewed prescription. Ask the team to coordinate supervised monthly testing and supply so that these safeguards are maintained.

chapters.title: Questions, decisions and practical support
chapters.intro: Your priorities and the burden of treatment belong in the discussion.

items.title: Benefits and uncertainties
items.text: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

items.title: Alternatives and review points
items.text: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.

items.title: Help with daily life
items.text: Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.

items.title: Shared understanding
items.text: Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.

chapters.title: Follow-up and your continuing record
chapters.intro: Keep this record when treatment is paused, changed or completed.

items.title: Your follow-up plan
items.text: Follow-up covers the treated area and the rest of your skin. The team chooses examinations and scans for your situation. Vismodegib pregnancy-prevention and donation restrictions continue for the periods listed in your safety plan after the final dose.

items.title: Continuing medicine precautions
items.text: Agree continuing clinical/skin review, any response imaging and support for ongoing effects. The pregnancy-prevention, donation and breastfeeding restrictions continue after the last dose for their specified periods.

items.title: Treatment summary for other clinicians
items.text: Record the medicines and last dates, important reactions, any long-term hormone replacement or steroid taper, and the responsible oncology contact. Show this information in urgent care and to other specialists. A different treatment phase does not erase earlier toxicity.

items.title: The complete paper version
items.text: Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.
